chunks: How motors and solenoids work. The question: Describe how a motor/solenoid works.
Both devices rely on two facts: current in a wire makes a magnetic field, and a magnetic field pushes on a current-carrying wire.
A solenoid uses the field to pull an iron plunger. A motor places a coil in a magnetic field so the force turns it, and keeps flipping the current so the turning continues.
A spinning motor also makes a voltage of its own that pushes back.
Think of pushing a child on a playground roundabout. To keep it going, you must push at the right moment on each turn.
If you pushed the same way at the wrong moment, you would slow it down.
A brushed motor has a part called a commutator that does the timing: it flips the current in the coil every half turn so the push is always the same way around.
Force falls as 1 over g squared with gap and rises as I squared : at 2 mm the 0. 5 amps curve gives 0. 98 N, halving the current gives one quarter (0. 25 N).
Real solenoids saturate near zero gap, so the curve flattens at small g , and designers shape the plunger tip to get a flatter force-stroke curve.
Magnetic field (B): the region where magnets and currents feel force. Torque: a twisting force. In a brushed motor it is proportional to current ( tau equals K t I ).
Commutator: the switch on the rotor that reverses the coil current each half turn.
Back-EMF: the voltage a spinning motor generates, proportional to speed, that opposes the supply. Air gap: the space the plunger has to close.
A solenoid's pull is strongest when it is small.
A solenoid has 500 turns, 0. 5 amps, a 1 cm² plunger and a 2 mm gap. The pull is about 1 N. Shrinking the gap to 1 mm makes it about 4 N, so a solenoid pulls harder as it closes.
For a motor with K t equals 0. 009 N·m/A, a current of 2 amps gives a torque of 0. 009 times 2 equals 0. 018 N·m. As the motor speeds up, back-EMF rises and the current falls.
That is the whole idea.
"Both use the fact that current makes a magnetic field and a field pushes on current.
A solenoid is a coil with an iron plunger that the field pulls in to close the air gap, with a spring to return it; force grows with turns times current and gets much stronger as the gap shrinks.
A brushed motor has a rotor coil in a magnet's field, so F equals BIL on each side gives torque proportional to current, and the commutator flips the current so torque stays one way.
The spinning coil also makes a back-EMF proportional to speed."
